questions.question: Outline the shape of world population growth over the last ten thousand years, explain what caused the explosion after 1800, and explain how the total can still be rising while the growth rate falls.
questions.expected_answer: For roughly ten millennia population barely grew: high birth rates were cancelled by almost equally high death rates from harvest failure, epidemics and infant deaths, so the world reached one billion only around 1804. Then the curve turned vertical: two billion by 1927, three billion by 1960, and then roughly a new billion every dozen years — 1974, 1987, 1999, 2011 and eight billion in 2022 — producing a J-curve with a long flat tail, an elbow around 1800 and a near-vertical climb. The cause was not rising births, which hardly moved at first, but collapsing deaths: better farming and transport increased food, while piped water, sanitation, vaccination and antibiotics disarmed the mass killers. Death rates plunged while births stayed high for a generation or more, so natural increase widened dramatically, especially after 1950 when a century of medical advances reached Africa, Asia and Latin America within one generation. The growth rate peaked near two percent in the late 1960s and has since fallen below one percent, yet the total still rises because a falling positive rate still adds people, and because of momentum: the enormous cohorts born in high-fertility decades are now parents, so even small average families produce many births. Projections show the line flattening beyond ten billion late this century — the J becoming an S.

questions.question: Define overpopulation and carrying capacity, use Singapore and southern Madagascar to show why overpopulation is not the same as density, and describe the symptoms by which an overpopulated region is recognised.
questions.expected_answer: A region is overpopulated when its population exceeds its carrying capacity — the maximum number of people the area's resources and technology can sustain at a reasonable standard of living. Overpopulation is a relationship between people and resources, while density is only a headcount per unit area. Singapore squeezes over eight thousand people onto each square kilometre, yet is not overpopulated because a wealthy, high-technology trading economy imports what its land cannot grow and sustains its citizens at a high standard. The far south of Madagascar carries only scattered people, yet in drought years it is genuinely overpopulated because meagre rainfall and exhausted soils mean even a sparse population outstrips what the land can renew, and hunger follows. The symptoms of strain: family plots shaved smaller with each inheritance and cultivation creeping onto slopes and marginal land; overgrazed pasture, trees felled for firewood, gully erosion and falling water tables; more job-seekers each year than jobs; oversubscribed classrooms, clinics and taps, with informal housing spreading faster than infrastructure; and finally hunger in bad years and outmigration of the young. Carrying capacity also moves: irrigation, fertiliser and improved seed raise the ceiling, while erosion, salinisation and emptied aquifers lower it — so a district can cross into overpopulation through resource loss alone, without any population growth.

questions.question: Evaluate the strategies for managing population growth, contrasting China's one-child policy with the voluntary routes taken by Bangladesh and Botswana, and place South Africa's experience in that debate.
questions.expected_answer: The strategies that work best widen people's choices. The strongest is educating girls and women: schooling delays marriage and first birth, opens ambitions beyond child-raising, brings income that makes each child's education a protected investment, and makes family planning knowledge usable — no measure moves birth rates further or more durably. Second, cutting infant mortality: where many babies die, parents keep extra children as insurance, so when immunisation, clean water and clinics make survival normal, family size falls within a generation. Third, family planning within physical and financial reach. Fourth, poverty reduction and social security, especially pensions, which end children's role as a retirement plan. China's one-child policy, enforced with fines from 1979 to 2015, cut births but left an ageing society before it grew wealthy, a shrinking workforce and a sex ratio skewed by son preference, with millions more boys than girls; official encouragement since the policy ended has barely lifted the birth rate. Bangladesh cut fertility from around six children per woman to near two through village-level family planning workers, girls' schooling and child health, and Botswana more than halved fertility through sustained investment in education and clinics — both without coercion and without demographic scars, showing choice matches force on results and beats it on consequences. South Africa belongs in the voluntary column: fertility fell from about six children per woman in the 1960s to roughly 2,3 today through urbanisation, women's education, clinic-based family planning and safer infancy, leaving growth near one percent and still easing.
